It sounds like you have a clear picture of the ultimate goal: using that terabyte-capable NAS to act as your data vault, while keeping your active workspace lean with a fast "thumbnail index" system rather than drowning in massive image files right away.

Building an automated system to pull everything down sequentially while grabbing lightweight reference thumbnails is a smart, measured way to handle a massive library. Let's design Step 1: The Automated Pipeline.

The Core Blueprint: API vs. Takeout

To automate this properly, we have to look at the two pathways Google provides, because they heavily impact your "lean thumbnail" strategy.

Option A: The Python Script + Google Photos API (Highly Automated)

This is the closest match to your vision. Using a script, you can interact with your library over the cloud sequentially.

  • How it works: A Python script requests your media items from Google. The API returns a baseUrl for every single image.
  • The Thumbnail Advantage: By appending formatting tags directly to the API's URL (e.g., baseUrl=w256-h256-c), Google automatically crops and scales the image. You can download a high-speed, tiny $256 \times 256$ pixel thumbnail directly to your indexing system.
  • The Big Capture: The script can then immediately pull the full-resolution version and stream it directly into your NAS network share directory.
  • The Caveat: The Google Photos API strips out some original metadata (like exact GPS coordinates) on the full-res download for privacy reasons.

Option B: The Takeout + Local Processing Engine (Data Complete)

If preserving 100% untouched metadata is a priority, Google Takeout is the standard choice, but we can adapt it to fit your lean indexing approach.

  • How it works: You request a 50GB zip package chunk from Google Takeout.
  • The Automation: Instead of sorting them by hand, you point an automated script or tool (like a Docker container running on your NAS) at the download folder.
  • The Thumbnail Advantage: The script extracts the full-res image directly into your NAS storage vault, instantly processes it locally to generate a low-res thumbnail, saves that thumbnail into your index system, and clears the cache.

Step 1 Action Plan: Building the Pipeline

Given that you want it simple, lean, and automated, here is how we can set up the infrastructure on your NAS.

1. Set Up Your NAS Target Shares

Create two distinct directories on your NAS to handle the separation of data:

  • /volume1/Photos_Vault/ – This is where your automated script will dump the heavy, full-resolution master files.
  • /volume1/Photos_Index/ – This is your lean workspace. It will only hold the ultra-lightweight thumbnails mapped exactly to the structure of the Vault.

2. Choose Your Automation Tool

Depending on your comfort level with code, you have two great paths forward to map the Google environment to your NAS:

Path 1: Python Automation (The API Route)

You can use a script using the google-auth and google-api-python-client libraries.

  • The script asks for your photos in batches of 100.
  • It downloads the thumbnail: image_url + "=w300" straight to /Photos_Index/.
  • It downloads the master file: image_url + "=d" straight to /Photos_Vault/.

Path 2: Containerized Sync (The Local-Processing Route)

If you prefer not to write scripts from scratch, you can run a tool like rclone via Docker directly on your NAS.

  • rclone has a dedicated Google Photos integration.
  • You can set up a command-line cron job on the NAS that sequentially fetches images item-by-item to limit network congestion.

To make sure we tailor the automated script or setup perfectly for Step 1, how comfortable are you with running a Python script or spinning up a Docker container/command-line tool directly on your NAS?

You hit the nail on the head. Google is incredibly aggressive with automated scraping detection on standard web endpoints, and their standard API limits will absolutely throw a wrench in a simple, continuous Python script if you try to pull 110 GB in one single go.

Here is the truth about the math, the costs, and how to avoid the "scraping wall."

The GCP Cost & Quota Realities

1. Financial Cost: $0.00

Using the Google Photos Library API/Picker API is free for personal development. Google does not charge you a per-gigabyte egress fee or a pay-per-request fee for using their Photos API. Your wallet is safe—it won't cost you $4, and it certainly won't cost you more.

2. The Hard Wall: The Quota Limit

While it won't cost money, Google caps your API usage strictly to prevent server strain:

  • The Library API limit is 10,000 requests per project per day for listing/organizing.
  • The Media Byte limit (actually downloading the image data via the baseUrl) is capped at 75,000 requests per project per day.

If you have tens of thousands of pictures, a naive loop in Python will hit a 429 Too Many Requests error and hard-halt your script long before it finishes your 110 GB library.

The Solution: A Frictionless, Cost-Free Hybrid Strategy

Since your main goal is an automated, simple pipeline that moves files step-by-step into the NAS without dealing with strict API throttling or proxy-evasion, the cleanest way forward is to separate Metadata Discovery from Heavy Data Fetching.

Instead of trying to force Python to download 110 GB of raw media bytes over a restricted API pipe, you can use Google's official, high-speed backbone to handle the heavy lifting, and let your script focus entirely on the indexing automation.

Phase 1: The "Bulk Dump" via Google Takeout

Instead of scraping, you let Google compile your 110 GB package on their own servers.

  1. Go to Google Takeout, uncheck everything except Google Photos, and request your export.
  2. Set the split size to 50 GB chunks so you only have 2 or 3 large zip files to download.
  3. Download those zip files directly into an /incoming_staging/ folder on your NAS.

Phase 2: The Local Automation Script (Zero Risk, Zero Throttle)

Now, because the files are already sitting locally on your NAS, your Python script can run entirely offline. There is zero risk of a ban, zero rate-limiting, and zero cost.

You can write a lightweight Python script that runs locally on the NAS to do the exact job you wanted:

[Google Takeout Zip Files]
          │
          ▼ (Python Local Script)
    ┌─────┴────────────────────────────────┐
    ▼                                      ▼
[/Photos_Vault/]                       [/Photos_Index/]
(Original 110GB Full-Res Files)        (Tiny, fast 256x256 thumbnails)
  1. Unzip & Traverse: It unpacks the images sequentially.
  2. Move to Vault: It moves the untouched, full-resolution file (complete with its native EXIF metadata) into /volume1/Photos_Vault/.
  3. Generate Thumbnail: It uses a standard Python library (like Pillow) to scale the image down to a tiny, lean 256px thumbnail and saves it into /volume1/Photos_Index/.

This gives you your exact indexing system step-by-step, keeps the NAS as your central command, and keeps Google's scraping alarms completely silent.

Yes, absolutely. For a 110 GB library, Google Takeout is by far the most stable, ban-proof, and completely free foundation you can build on. It lets Google’s massive servers do the grinding work of assembling the data packaging, leaving you with just a few clean files to download directly to your storage space.

Before you kick off the export, there are two critical settings you need to toggle to save yourself a massive headache later during the automation phase.

1. Configure the Takeout Request Correctly

When you go to Google Takeout and deselect everything except Google Photos, scroll down to the bottom before hitting "Next Step" and match these settings:

  • File Type: .zip
  • File Size: 50 GB

    Why this matters: By default, Google sets this to 2 GB. For 110 GB, that means you'd have to manually download 55 individual zip files. Setting it to 50 GB means Google will package your entire library into just 2 or 3 large zip files. It’s much cleaner to automate.

2. Heads Up: The "Google JSON" Quirk

There is one big catch with Google Takeout that trips up almost everyone trying to parse it with a script: Google splits the metadata.

When you unzip a Takeout folder, you'll see a structure like this:

📂 Photos from 2024/
 ├── 📄 IMG_4832.jpg        <-- The actual image file
 └── 📄 IMG_4832.jpg.json   <-- The "sidecar" metadata file

Google strips things like custom descriptions, tags, and edited timestamps out of the raw image and writes them into that companion .json file. Furthermore, if an image has a really long name, Google truncates the name of the .json file so it doesn't perfectly match the image name anymore.

Next Step: Preparing the Local Automation Script

While Google compiles your zip files (which usually takes a few hours to a day), we can sketch out the Python local script that will run directly on your NAS.

Because we are doing this locally, our Python automation will:

  1. Traverse the extracted Takeout folders.
  2. Match each image to its truncated .json sidecar to extract the true "Date Taken."
  3. Move the pristine full-res file into /volume1/Photos_Vault/.
  4. Generate the fast, ultra-lightweight thumbnail into /volume1/Photos_Index/.
